CausalChain: Oxidative stress in liver cells -> Activation of mTOR/TBK1 kinases -> Phosphorylation of p62 at Ser349 and modulation of MOAP-1 regulation -> Enhanced p62 binding to Keap1 -> Disruption of Keap1-mediated Nrf2 degradation -> Transient accumulation and nuclear translocation of Nrf2 -> Upregulation of antioxidant/detoxification genes -> (If sustained) chronic p62 accumulation leading to metabolic reprogramming, fibrosis, and tumorigenesis
Hypothesis: We hypothesize that by simultaneously modulating p62 phosphorylation at Ser349 and regulating the adjunct MOAP-1 pathway through CRISPR-based phosphomutant strategies, in coordination with precisely timed kinase modulator delivery via microfluidic systems, it is possible to finely tune the p62–Keap1–Nrf2 axis in hepatocytes. This integrated approach will allow a controlled, transient activation of Nrf2—sufficient for cytoprotection against oxidative stress—while preventing the deleterious consequences of chronic Nrf2 overactivation that drive metabolic reprogramming, liver fibrosis, and tumorigenesis. The incorporation of advanced real-time phosphoproteomic and multi-omics analyses will provide quantifiable, dynamic metrics to differentiate between beneficial transient responses and harmful sustained activation, thereby optimizing the therapeutic interventions in liver disease.
Abstract: We propose that a combinatorial approach integrating selective modulation of p62 phosphorylation at Ser349 with concurrent regulation of the p62-associated MOAP-1 axis via CRISPR-engineered phosphomutants, targeted kinase modulators, and real-time multi-omics monitoring can precisely control the p62–Keap1–Nrf2 signaling cascade in hepatocytes. By employing microfluidic systems for temporal delivery of kinase modulators and advanced phosphoproteomic analyses, this strategy aims to induce a well-defined, transient surge in Nrf2 activity that confers cytoprotection against oxidative stress, while preventing the chronic overactivation linked to metabolic reprogramming, liver fibrosis, and tumorigenesis. This dual-targeted paradigm refines the mechanistic intervention through broader regulatory oversight—addressing both p62 phosphorylation and MOAP-1 mediated control of p62 body accumulation—and offers a robust framework for therapeutic modulation in liver disease.
Orignal_vs_New: The original hypothesis focused solely on selective modulation of p62 phosphorylation at Ser349 to control Nrf2 activity using kinase modulators and CRISPR-based phosphomutants along with advanced omics analyses. In the revised hypothesis, we have expanded the approach by incorporating the regulation of the MOAP-1 axis—a known negative regulator of p62 body accumulation—and by employing additional contemporary technologies such as microfluidic systems for precise temporal control. These enhancements provide broader control over the p62–Keap1–Nrf2 signaling pathway, address possible compensatory mechanisms, and enable real-time feedback to clearly distinguish transient, protective Nrf2 activation from chronic, pathological activation, thereby refining both the mechanistic understanding and practical implementability of the intervention.
